paper_title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.15.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.14.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.311.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.23.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Autoregressive (AR) language models generate left to right. This simple learning target scales effectively, but fixes the generation order, restricts attention to prior tokens, and produces only one new token per step. Diffusion language models (DLMs) instead iteratively reconstruct multiple positions in corrupted sequence using bidirectional context (Austin et al., 2021a; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024). Their number of function evaluations (NFE) can be chosen independently of output length, and early low-probability predictions can be revised. Training or adapting models for diffusive generation, however, has remained computationally intensive and expensive. Our primary aim is therefore compute-efficient, reproducible recipe for converting AR models into DLMs without pretraining diffusion foundation model for every architecture. This matters for three reasons. First, full diffusion pretraining is financially and environmentally costly: for example, under our standardized rental and electricity scenario, the reported LLaDA run corresponds to approximately $675,000 and 44,100 kg CO2e  (Table 1)  . It should be noted that these illustrative estimates are neither the authors bill nor measured emissions; operational carbon depends strongly on utilization, datacenter efficiency, location, and energy supply (Strubell et al., 2019; Patterson

Second, AR-to-DLM conversion in hours on one widely available cloud instance makes hands-on DLM research available beyond laboratories with multi-node clusters. Third, applying the same inexpensive intervention to multiple existing model families makes it feasible to study how architecture and parent-model choice affect diffusion generation without repeating foundation-model pretraining for every comparison. We study this question with BYOD, generalizable conversion and evaluation pipeline for four instruction-tuned decoder families: Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B. We selected the latest, comparably sized text-only instruction checkpoints to avoid modality-specific confounding. Every backbone receives the same bidirectional attention intervention, LoRA target modules, and masked-diffusion objective. This paired design separates conversion quality from the strength of the starting checkpoint. We directly compare our models against LLaDA 8B Instruct because its standard masked-diffusion objective, instruction-tuning setup, and overlapping benchmark suite make it the cleanest external reference baseline. We additionally report published DiffuLLaMA, Dream-Instruct, iLLaDA-Instruct, and Efficient-DLM values, but keep them protocol-separated: their additional attention, masking, scheduling, data, and inference techniques would confound controlled comparison. Our contributions are: compute-efficient recipe that converts four instruction-tuned AR model families to masked diffusion using only few single-GPU hours and LoRA parameter updates; paired evaluation of each diffusion model and its frozen AR parent across general knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, and code benchmarks; controlled analysis of training duration, denoising-step count, validation loss, perplexity and distinct n-grams; and standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four models, supporting accessible DLM conversion and qualitative evaluation.

MDLM and contemporaneous work showed that this masked formulation admits simple noise-weighted crossentropy objective, while RADD reparameterized the predictor in terms of conditional distributions over clean tokens (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025). These approaches form the basis of masked diffusion language models (MDLMs). Uniform (or multinomial) diffusion, which instead corrupts tokens with samples from the ordinary vocabulary, is another option (Hoogeboom et al., 2021); we use the simpler absorbing-mask denoising objective employed by LLaDA. The authors of LLaDA were the first to scale masked diffusion to an 8B general-purpose language model (Nie et al., 2025). Its architecture follows Llama 3.1 8B, but it was pretrained from scratch using 2.3T tokens and 130,000 GPU-hours. AR-to-diffusion conversion instead reuses knowledge from an AR checkpoint. DiffuLLaMA established this route through 65B tokens of full-model continued training at 7B scale (Gong et al., 2025). Dream uses DiffuLLaMAs shifted-prediction initialization, continues Qwen2.5 for 580B tokens, and adds context-adaptive token-level noise rescheduling (Ye et al., 2025). Efficient-DLM combines 500B tokens of continued training with blockwise attention and position-dependent masking (Fu et al., 2025), whereas iLLaDA uses fromscratch diffusion pretraining at substantially larger scale (Nie et al., 2026). Conversion has also reached larger sparse models through RND1 (30B parameters), LLaDA2.0 (16B and 100B), and DiffusionGemma (25.2B, using uniform diffusion) (Chandrasegaran et al., 2025; Bie et al., 2025; DiffusionGemma Team, 2026). Thus, Gemma-, Llama-, and Qwen-based diffusion models were already reported, but we found no prior diffusion conversion of Ministral 8B Instruct 2410. Hybrid and blockwise models offer different compromise between bidirectionality and deployability. Block Diffusion is autoregressive across blocks but diffusive within each block, enabling variablelength generation and inter-block KV caching (Arriola et al., 2025). Fast-dLLM v2 converts Qwen2.5 models using full-parameter fine-tuning with approximately 1B tokens and combines blockwise complementary masking with hierarchical caching (Wu et al., 2025). These systems retain more left-to-right structure than our fully bidirectional answer block, making them especially relevant to speed, caching, and arbitrary-length generation but not suited as direct controls for our intervention. LAD first showed that LoRA can induce diffusion generation, using hybrid objective that combines masking with token swaps, duplications, and span shifts (Kuiper et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2022). However, BYOD instead tests whether simpler IID absorbing-mask objective can transfer reliably across model families. Other LoRA-based diffusion work addresses different goals: Uno learns diffusion-draft adapters while retaining the AR model as verifier, the dLLM framework uses LoRA to fine-tune already-diffusive checkpoints rather than for its Tiny-A2D conversion, and NaRA adapts existing diffusion models with noise-conditioned LoRA (Sahoo et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Thus, their LoRA components augment already diffusively generating models, rather than converting AR model families into standalone diffusion models. Table 1 compares training budgets for similarly sized diffusion models. For AR-to-diffusion conversion methods, these budgets exclude the substantial earlier cost of training the AR parent; for from-scratch methods they include diffusion pretraining. Dollar and operational-emissions columns are rental-equivalent estimates under one documented pricing and energy scenario, not the authors actual bills or measured footprints; Appendix gives the complete calculation and its limitations.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: 3.1 MASKED-DIFFUSION TRAINING OBJECTIVE The training objective teaches the adapted model to reconstruct masked response tokens while conditioning on an uncorrupted instruction. 0, . . . , xL Let be the instruction, x0 = (x1 0 ) the clean response region, the answer positions, and the EOS-padding positions. For each example, we sample U[103, 1] and independently mask each position in with probability t, yielding the corrupted sequence xt and masked set Mt. For either region {A, }, we calculate the same-position reconstruction loss ℓR(θ) = 1 tR (cid:88) iMtR log pϕ,θ(xi 0 p, xt). (1) We then combine the answer and padding losses: L(θ) = Et,x0,xt [0.9ℓA(θ) + 0.1ℓP (θ)] . Here, pϕ,θ is the conditional token distribution, ϕ denotes the frozen parent parameters, and θ the LoRA parameters. The first terminating EOS is included as genuine answer token; all subsequent EOS tokens are treated as padding. The factor 1/t corrects for the sampled masking rate. Prompt and chat-template tokens remain visible to the model and are not part of the loss. Training masks are resampled online; validation masks are fixed by example index and seed. (2) 3.2 AUTOREGRESSIVE-TO-DIFFUSION CONVERSION To convert an autoregressive model to diffusion-style model, we replace the causal mask in every layer with bidirectional attention mask, so every prompt, answer, and EOS-padding position can attend to every position. We attach LoRA adapters to every self-attention query and value projection, with rank = 1024, scaling α = 1024, and dropout zero. The rest of the model architecture and output vocabulary remain unchanged. Backbone weights, token embeddings, the language-model head, biases, and normalization layers are frozen. The pretrained output head is also retained unchanged: whereas autoregressive training compares each positions logits with the next token through shifted labels, BYOD removes this label shift and predicts the clean token at the same position from the bidirectionally attended, corrupted sequence. Each model reuses an existing singletoken string from its tokenizer (MASK for Gemma, Llama, and Qwen; <?> for Ministral), avoiding vocabulary expansion. We fix the LoRA rank across model families to retain one architecture-independent recipe. Matching trainable parameter counts would require model-specific ranks and would still not control for differences in depth, width, and attention design. This results in variation in trainable parameters, which is therefore potential confounder in cross-family comparisons. Every conversion was trained on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU in Google Colab, without distributed parallelism; Table 2 reports parameter counts and conversion times.

sections.title: 3.3 TRAINING DATA
sections.content: We construct one-million-example mixture containing 45% general instruction following, 18% multiple-choice reasoning, 18% mathematics, and 19% code. Within these groups, the source weights are: Clean-Instruct-3M/Tulu 3/Alpaca-GPT4/Alpaca at 40/35/20/5 (Crumb, 2023; Lambert et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2023a; Taori et al., 2023); MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC-Easy at 73/25/2 (Hendrycks et al., 2021a; Zellers et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2018); Orca-Math/GSM8K at 95/5 (Mitra et al., 2024; Cobbe et al., 2021); and OpenCoder/MBPP at 99.7/0.3 (Huang et al., 2024; Austin et al., 2021b). When applicable, only the training splits are used. We deduplicate normalized prompts, exclude exact matches with held-out benchmark prompts, and retain only examples that fit the 256-token training length. Each model receives the same shuffled examples, retokenized with its native chat template and tokenizer. Prompt tokens remain clean; only answer and EOS-padding positions can be corrupted. The four primary models see the same dataset prefix. BYOD-Llama-50k uses the same fixed shuffle for longer, 800,000-example run with newly sampled corruptions. Exact run sizes and optimization settings are given in Appendix C. 3.4 INFERENCE Inference begins from fixed-length, fully masked answer block. At each denoising step, the model predicts all masked positions, retains the most confident predictions, and remasks lower-confidence positions; accepted tokens remain unmasked. This can resolve several output tokens per network evaluation. Task-specific lengths, denoising budgets, temperatures, and EOS/EOT handling are given in Appendix D.

sections.title: 4 EVALUATION
sections.content: 4.1 PAIRED MODELS AND BASELINES We refer to the four conversions as BYOD-Gemma, BYOD-Qwen, BYOD-Ministral, and BYODLlama. For Llama, we distinguish the primary and longer-trained checkpoints as BYOD-Llama-25k and BYOD-Llama-50k. We also compare each model with its unchanged AR parent. LLaDA 8B Instruct serves as an external diffusion baseline in the same harness; results reported by other papers are presented separately because their protocols differ. We specifically use BYOD-Llama for the longer run and checkpoint-wise analysis because DiffuLLaMA, LLaDA, and iLLaDA use Llama or closely related Llama-style architectures, making it the clearest basis for comparison with prominent general-purpose DLMs (Gong et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2025; 2026). We also compare BYOD-Llama25k before and after folding its LoRA weights into the base model, to see if merging deteriorates the results. The nine standard task benchmarks use greedy token selection and low-confidence remasking, while open-ended generation uses temperature 0.7 and delayed EOS/EOT acceptance. Complete settings are reported in Appendix D.

We score multiple-choice tasks by option label, GSM8K by its final number, MATH by its normalized final boxed expression, and code tasks by whether the generated program passes the supplied tests in an isolated subprocess. 4.3 OPEN-ENDED GENERATION We assess output fluency with perplexity and Distinct-1/2/3 calculated over answers on 100 openended questions. Standard masked diffusion does not directly provide the left-to-right sequence likelihood used for AR perplexity, and its usual evidence lower bound is not proper test-time likelihood (Turok et al., 2026). We therefore follow prior DLM work and use frozen Microsoft Phi-4 14B as an external perplexity scorer (Gong et al., 2025). We pool negative log-likelihoods across all non-padding tokens of all generated answers before exponentiating, so every token has equal weight. Because this score does not measure diversity, we also report sliding model-token Distinct-1/2/3 percentages after removing special tokens. Higher Distinct-n indicates less local repetition (Li et al., 2016); in our experiments, it exposed cases where perplexity improved because output became more repetitive rather than better. 4.4 BIDIRECTIONAL ATTENTION TEST We test whether the converted diffusion models allow bidirectional information flow with simple right-context copy task (Appendix G). Most of the response is pre-filled, and the model must fill an earlier masked position by copying word shown later in the response. causal model cannot change its prediction at an earlier position based on later token, so sensitivity to this clue directly tests functional bidirectional attention. Figure 2 shows one test item and its expected reconstruction.

sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: 5.1 BENCHMARK ACCURACY AND BASE-MODEL DEPENDENCE Table 3 shows that BYOD-Gemma has the highest BYOD average and comes within 1.3 points of LLaDA in the matched harness. The AR parents perform better on average, but the conversion gap varies by task and backbone. Extending BYOD-Llama from 25,000 to 50,000 updates raises its average by 0.5 points, with gains on five tasks and declines on four. Figure 1 shows the largest gaps with AR in mathematics and code. On paired HumanEval/MBPP subsets, parsing failed for 28.0%/8.8% of BYOD-Llama-50k outputs versus 0%/0% for Llama AR (Appendix E). LLaDA scores 2.6 points below its published average in our harness, illustrating protocol sensitivity; other external comparisons appear in Appendix H. The merged BYOD-Llama remains broadly similar across factual and open-generation measures (Appendix B). 5.2 OPEN-ENDED GENERATION Figure 3 shows that perplexity and Distinct-1 generally improve with additional NFE. Appendix reports the exact values: across NFE budgets, converted models have 2.75.0 times their AR parents perplexity and generally lower Distinct-n. For simplicity, we discuss Distinct-1 in the main text; appendix results for Distinct-1/2/3 show the same broad pattern. LLaDA also has lower perplexity than every BYOD model. Representative samples are provided in Appendix to illustrate iterative refinement under different remasking strategies and NFE budgets. 5.3 FURTHER TRAINING The benchmark results show small but uneven accuracy gain from further training. Figure 4 shows that validation loss decreases almost monotonically and begins to plateau toward the end of 50,000 training updates. Perplexity also decreases across all NFE budgets, but with larger fluctuations between checkpoints. Distinct-1 changes comparatively little and remains broadly stable. BYODLlama perplexity remains well above LLaDA, whose perplexity is in turn above the Llama AR baseline. In contrast, BYOD-Llama and LLaDA have similar Distinct-1 scores, while the AR baseline remains higher. 5.4 BIDIRECTIONAL ATTENTION TEST Adding the later clue changed the greedy prediction on 100% of test items for every converted model and LLaDA, confirming that all models use right-context information. sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: The central result is that high-rank attention-only LoRA can convert four AR models into DLMs in few hours on single GPU. The converted models do not surpass their AR parents on average, but do approach another DLM, LLaDA, on benchmark accuracy. This demonstrates that the conversion is feasible and effective, even if it does not fully close the performance gap. Several aspects of these findings warrant closer examination, and are discussed below. Conversion quality varies by backbone: BYOD-Gemma performs best on benchmark tasks despite Qwen having the strongest AR parent, so parent capability alone does not determine conversion quality. Gemmas larger model and adapter budget may contribute, but cannot be separated here. The largest benchmark deficits relative to the AR parents occur in mathematics and code. In code, parser checks and qualitative inspection reveal syntactic errors, which do not occur in AR answers (Appendix E). This is consistent with prior work showing that parallel token prediction in DLMs can produce syntactic inconsistencies (Hersche et al., 2026). Although generation under full NFE budgets generally produces coherent sentences, perplexity and Distinct-1/2/3 still trail both the AR parents and LLaDA, especially when NFE is below output length. This is also noticeable qualitatively when using the models through the demo interface. Extending Llama training from 25,000 to 50,000 updates yields marginal average factual-accuracy gain, with improvements on some tasks offset by declines on others. While validation loss still decreases almost monotonically during the longer run, these downstream results suggest that longer training alone may

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: be insufficient; useful ablations would include larger effective batches, alternative denoising targets, and adapters in key/output projections, MLPs, or normalization layers. Even though we used perplexity and Distinct-1/2/3 as proxies for fluency, they are not sufficient to reliably predict human preference. For example, an external AR perplexity scoring model can favor repetitive high-probability text. While Distinct-n captures this repetition, these metrics still do not measure factuality, grammar, or coherence (Gong et al., 2025; Turok et al., 2026). We therefore combine perplexity, Distinct-1/2/3, task accuracy, and demos for qualitative inspection of generated samples, rather than treating any one metric as definitive. In the bidirectionality test, every converted model changed its prediction on every item when the later clue was added, demonstrating bidirectional attention across all four families. Some models did not always copy the token correctly, indicating failure to use the clue rather than an absence of information flow. The public demos enable quick experimentation with NFE, output length, remasking, and blockwise generation, while exposing grammaticality, coherence, and denoising errors that aggregate metrics cannot capture. LoRA keeps all original parameters frozen during conversion, preventing their direct overwriting and potentially reducing catastrophic forgetting (Luo et al., 2023). We adopt = 1024 as fixed transfer setting rather than claiming that it is minimal or optimal; systematically characterizing the rankqualitycompute trade-off remains future work. However, prior diffusion adaptation work also favored higher ranks over smaller ones (Kuiper et al., 2025). It should be noted that the high-rank adapters can subsequently be merged into the base projections. This removes their temporary parameter and inference overhead while restoring the original model size with broadly similar behavior, as shown by our experiments (Appendix B). Future work could study whether merged models could subsequently initialize partial or full diffusion fine-tuning; establishing diffusion generation before exposing the original weights to optimization may make these updates less disruptive. Finally, although one conversion takes only few hours, development and evaluation across models, configurations, ablations, and validation runs required hundreds of GPU-hours. Nevertheless, BYOD reuses an AR checkpoint and processes orders of magnitude fewer token positions than the full-model systems in Table 1, enabling repeatable cross-architecture experiments without repeated pretraining. This does not erase the original pretraining cost or establish proportional reduction in emissions.

sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: The main limitation is that efficient conversion does not yet produce efficient generation, as output quality is not yet on par with the AR parents or LLaDA, especially when NFE is below output length. We also measure inference budget in network evaluations rather than wall-clock latency. Fewer sequential evaluations do not guarantee speedup because each diffusion step processes the full answer block. Our efficiency claim therefore concerns training the conversion, not measured inference acceleration. The cross-backbone comparison is not controlled architecture study. The parents differ in size, tokenizer, pretraining, alignment, and attention design. Fixing LoRA rank also gives each backbone different absolute adapter budget. Gemmas leading result therefore cannot be attributed separately to architecture, parent quality, model size, or trainable parameter count. Finally, the automatic generation metrics cover only part of text quality. Phi-4 perplexity reflects the preferences of an external AR model, while Distinct-n detects local repetition but not factuality, grammar, or coherence. Published results from other DLMs use different protocols; only LLaDA was rerun in our harness. We also did not measure energy use or carbon intensity directly, so claims on cost or resource efficiency should only be taken as indicative of relative scale rather than measured (environmental) footprint.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: BYOD converts instruction-tuned AR checkpoints across four families into bidirectional masked generators in few hours on one Google Colab GPU while retaining substantial parent-model

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: knowledge. Fluency and diversity nevertheless trail the AR parents and LLaDA, especially when NFE is below output length. promising next step is partial or full diffusion fine-tuning initialized from the merged model, testing whether quality can improve without eroding retained capabilities. BYOD thereby enables rapid, controlled diffusion experiments across established model families with minimal compute infrastructure.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The standalone implementation is available at https://github.com/RuurdKuiper/BYOD, with Colab training notebook, revision-pinned training presets, inference and adapter merging, and the benchmark evaluation harness. Full-precision ZeroGPU demos are provided for all four conversions. The main text specifies the objective, trainable modules, data volume, optimization, generation, benchmarks, and scoring. The repository documents release scope and configuration provenance; new training run does not guarantee bitwise reproduction of the reported checkpoints or scores.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This study uses existing language models and public benchmark or instruction datasets and does not involve human subjects. Converted models inherit factual errors, biases, unsafe behaviors, licensing constraints, and memorization risks from their parent checkpoints and training data. We report aggregate task performance rather than claiming safety or deployment readiness; release artifacts should preserve upstream licenses and document the data provenance and intended research use.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used to assist software development and debugging, creation of analysis scripts, literature discovery and summarization, creation of the open-ended question dataset, and drafting and editing this manuscript. The authors manually reviewed AI-assisted code and prose, and verified literature claims and citations against primary sources. No benchmark value was entered solely from an unsupported model response. The authors take responsibility for the final content, claims, code, and artifacts.

COST AND OPERATIONAL-EMISSIONS ESTIMATION Table 1 compares the cost of training model that produces diffusion behavior. It should thus be taken into account that some of these models build on an AR parent, whereas others are trained from scratch. It also excludes exploratory runs, failed jobs, dataset construction, evaluation, storage, and inference. The estimates must therefore not be interpreted as total project or lifecycle footprints.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: For BYOD we use the observed 3.2 GPU-hours for the conversion of Llama 3.1 8B model for diffusive generation. For prior work that reports GPU-hours, we retain that value. Where paper reports model size but not time, we approximate training compute as 6N FLOPs (Hoffmann et al., 2022), where is total training compute, is the number of model parameters, and is the number of processed training-token positions. We then calculate Gest = 6N 0.40 (989 1012) 3600 , (3) where Gest is aggregate estimated GPU-hours, 0.40 is the assumed model FLOPs utilization (MFU), 989 1012 is the NVIDIA H100s dense BF16 Tensor Core throughput in FLOP/s (NVIDIA, 2023), and 3600 converts seconds to hours. The 40% MFU assumption is consistent with the 39.045.0% BF16 MFUs reported by FP8-LM for GPT-style 7B, 13B, and 175B training on H100 GPUs (Peng et al., 2023b). Actual utilization varies considerably with architecture, sequence length, parallelization, communication, activation recomputation, and implementation efficiency. The assumption is therefore standardized order-of-magnitude convention rather than reconstruction of any authors cluster. It yields the daggered values in Table 1. The Dream and iLLaDA estimates cover their main 580Band 12T-token stages but omit the smaller instruction-tuning additions, so they are lower bounds. Table 4 calibrates the same calculation against studies that report both usable token count and elapsed accelerator-hours (Nie et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). For LLaDA, it predicts approximately 77,519 GPU-hours, compared with 130,000 reported H800 GPU-hours, corresponding to an implied utilization of 23.9%. Thus 40% can be optimistic about achieved utilization and correspondingly conservative with respect to estimated accelerator-hours, rental cost, and emissions. Fast-dLLM v2 displays still larger gap. Its specialized training concatenates clean and noised views and uses nonstandard attention pattern, illustrating that an implied MFU from 6N is calibration diagnostic, not measured hardware-utilization statistic. Table 4: Calibration of the 6N estimator against reported accelerator-hours. Predictions use 40% MFU and the stated accelerators dense-BF16 peak (989 TFLOP/s H100-class proxy for H800; 312 TFLOP/s for A100) (NVIDIA, 2023; 2021). Implied MFU is the utilization that would reconcile 6N with reported time; it is not measured MFU. System Parameters Tokens Pred. AWS specifies that this instance contains the same 96-GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU used in our Colab run (Amazon Web Services, 2026c;b). For other systems we use one consistent current major-cloud proxy: $5.191 per accelerator-hour for an AWS p5.4xlarge H100 Capacity Block in US East (Amazon Web Services, 2026a). Thus these figures answer what would the stated or estimated accelerator-hours cost at public contemporary rate?, not what the original authors paid. They exclude storage, egress, idle reservation time, taxes, and discounts. Operational emissions are estimated as energy use multiplied by the data centers power usage effectiveness (PUE) and the grid carbon intensity (Lannelongue et al., 2021; Patterson et al., 2021): (cid:98)ECO2e = PGPU PUE Igrid. (4) Here (cid:98)ECO2e is estimated operational emissions in kg CO2e, is aggregate GPU-hours, PGPU is assumed per-GPU power draw in kW, PUE is the dimensionless data-center power usage effectiveness, and Igrid is grid carbon intensity in kg CO2e/kWh. We use 0.60 kW for RTX PRO 6000 runs, matching NVIDIAs stated maximum board power (NVIDIA, 2025), and 0.70-kW H100-class proxy for all other entries except the reported A100 run, for which we use 0.40 kW (NVIDIA, 2023; 2021). We assume PUE 1.09, Googles reported fleet-wide value (Google Cloud, 2025), and the IEAs 2024 global-average generation intensity of 0.445 kg CO2e/kWh (International Energy Agency, 2025). ADAPTER-MERGING ABLATION High-rank LoRA increases the parameter count only while the adapter remains separate. To test whether removing this overhead changes behavior, we evaluate the same BYOD-Llama-25k checkpoint with the adapter loaded and after its weights are folded into the base projections. Tables 5 and 6 report open-generation and factual results, respectively. Table 5: Open-generation comparison of the adapter-loaded and merged Llama checkpoints. PPL is token-weighted; Distinct-n is averaged over answers and reported as percentage. Both use 128 generated tokens; D-1/2/3 use 32 NFE. Parameters Representation D-1% D-3% D-2% PPL128 PPL32 Adapter loaded Merged standalone 8.466B 8.030B 19.381 19. 5.081 4.764 49.5 49.8 78.8 80.7 89.9 91.8 Table 6: Factual benchmark accuracy (%) before and after merging in the matched harness; the mean is unweighted across the nine tasks. Task Adapter Merged Adapter Merged Task ARC-C GPQA GSM8K HellaSwag HumanEval 83.2 29.6 65.6 70.4 31.2 84.0 30.4 63.2 69.6 29.6 MATH MBPP MMLU MMLU-Pro Mean 25.6 43.2 59.2 30.4 48.7 24.8 41.6 60.8 30.4 48.3 Merging is an algebraic reparameterization rather than an additional training stage: each base projection is replaced by + (α/r)BA, where and are the trained rank-r LoRA matrices and α is their scaling parameter. Subject to floating-point rounding, evaluating the folded projection is equivalent to evaluating the base and LoRA branches separately. Open-generation metrics are slightly better after merging, while factual results vary modestly by task and the macro mean decreases by only 0.4 points. These reruns therefore support preservation of overall behavior, but are not precise enough to attribute task-level changes to merging; logit-level deterministic parity test would isolate numerical merge error from generation and benchmark variance.

sections.title: C COMPLETE TRAINING CONFIGURATION
sections.content: Table 7 records the common resolved configuration of the four primary conversions, including optimization, precision, checkpointing, and validation. We use AdamW with BF16 master weights and Transformer Engine HYBRID FP8 execution. The implementation pins the one-million-example training mixture Ruurd/LAD-training-1m-256 at revision 6041513b684d6ca627879ffdb547 b8629bb8b8de. BYOD-Llama-50k keeps the same batch size and objective but processes 800,000 examples over 50,000 updates, validates every 500 updates, and uses linear learning-rate decay from 105 to 106. This run supplies the BYOD-Llama-50k results and the diagnostics in Figure 4.

sections.title: G BIDIRECTIONAL ATTENTION TEST
sections.content: This deterministic test uses ordinary single-token target words. Each partial response has the form Answer:[MASK]. COPY: apple., with different target in each example. The target is absent from the instruction and left context and appears explicitly after the mask. The converted model predicts the masked position by greedy argmax in one forward pass; no iterative sampling or generation settings are involved. We score the same masked position twice: once with the later copy clue and once after deleting that clue. We report exact match for both conditions, their difference, and whether adding the clue changes the greedy prediction at all. Under causal attention, changing or deleting tokens to the right cannot affect logits at an earlier position, so both the exact-match gain and prediction-change rate must be zero. The latter separates use of right context from the stricter ability to follow the exact-copy instruction. This is functional attention check, not benchmark of reasoning or general infilling quality. Table 13 reports the results for both conditions.

sections.title: INTERACTIVE DENOISING TRAJECTORIES
sections.content: Figures 7 and 8 illustrate how the public BYOD-Gemma demo exposes the parallel refinement process under random and confidence-guided remasking. All panels use the displayed Amsterdam prompt, the helpful-assistant system prompt, temperature 0.7, top-k 3, initial noise fraction 1.0, delayed EOS/EOT retention, permanent locked retention, and no visualization delay. Early stopping is disabled and block length equals the new-token canvas, ensuring that every panel displays its complete denoising budget. The demo randomizes the hidden sampling seed for every request; we resample the 64-NFE conditions to show readable positive examples, so these trajectories illustrate behavior rather than constitute controlled quality comparison.
